intro: No European capital does ancient trees like London. Its oldest oaks survive thanks to royal appetite: kings walled off hunting parks for their deer, and the trees inside were left to grow old while the countryside around them was cleared. The city even gave its name to the London plane, the soot-proof hybrid that lines its streets. The trees here range from a churchyard yew older than Londinium to a plane valued at three quarters of a million pounds and a cedar the Beatles filmed under. All but Kew and Syon are free, though two Temple trees keep lawyers' hours.
meta_description: London's ancient trees stand in royal parks, churchyards and squares, from the Totteridge Yew, older than Londinium, to a cedar the Beatles filmed under.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in London?
faq.a: The Totteridge Yew in St Andrew's churchyard, Totteridge, estimated at between 1,000 and 2,000 years old. Even the cautious low estimate makes it older than any building in the city.

faq.q: Are London's ancient trees free to visit?
faq.a: All but two of the trees on this list are free: they stand in public parks, streets, churchyards, squares and forest. The exceptions are the Old Lions of Kew, which need a Kew Gardens ticket, and the Syon Park mulberries, inside Syon's ticketed grounds. The two Temple mulberries are free but open only on weekday lunchtimes.

faq.q: Why does London have so many ancient trees?
faq.a: Royal hunting parks. Kings walled off Richmond and Greenwich centuries ago, and the oaks inside were spared the clearing that transformed the surrounding countryside. Churchyards kept old yews too, from Totteridge to Harlington and Downe.
A hybrid plane tree that thrives on soot and hard pruning. London planted it everywhere from the 1700s on, and the tree took the city's name with it.
